newsitem.title: USA: Miami exile leader plans to enter Cuban waters.
newsitem.headline: Miami exile leader plans to enter Cuban waters.

text.p: The leader of a Cuban exile group said on Wednesday he would sail a small boat into Cuban waters in a protest to mark the anniversary of the drowning of 41 boatpeople fleeing the Communist-ruled island three years ago.
The U.S. Coast Guard said it was aware of the plan and was weighing its options, which could include halting the exile vessel before it leaves port in the Florida Keys on Sunday.
The planned incursion into Cuban waters is the latest confrontation between Miami's Cubans and President Fidel Castro's government, which views their protest flotillas as provocations.

Ramon Saul Sanchez, head of an exile group called Democracy Movement, said he would pilot a small boat to the site eight miles (13 km) north of Havana where a stolen Cuban tugboat called "Thirteen of March" sank on July 13, 1994.
The boat was packed with refugees and 41 died. Exiles say it was deliberately rammed by a Cuban naval ship and sprayed with high pressure hoses. Cuba says it was an accident.

Sanchez told Reuters he would carry a white rose, a copy of the Declaration of Human Rights and a message to Cuban authorities in a sealed container. "I will not in any way be threatening or disrepectful to anyone," he said. "This is a symbolic claim of our right to return to our country."

Cuba has warned organisers of past flotillas that any violation of its territory would not be tolerated and could be met with force. On Feb. 24, 1996, Cuban MiG fighters shot down two small civilian planes over international waters off Cuba, killing four Cuban American members of the Brothers to the Rescue group. Cuba said the planes had violated its airspace.
Under current law, anyone attempting to leave Florida in a small boat with intent to enter Cuban territory would need a permit, Coast Guard Lt. Cmdr. Marc Woodring said.
"We're very concerned for his safety," he said. "In the past the Cuban government has detained persons who have entered without permission."
Some 40 boats were expected to participate in Sunday's flotilla, the 11th such expedition to the edge of Cuban territorial waters.

Democracy Movement said it expected to conduct at least one more this year in advance of a massive flotilla during Pope John Paul II's visit to Cuba next January, at which time exile groups say they will exercise their right to enter Cuba.

Sanchez said his planned entry into Cuban waters was not intended to provoke Castro and compared it to civil rights heroine Rosa Parks' defiant refusal to sit at the back of buses during racial segregation in the United States.

"I expect them to try to prevent me from entering. My experience dealing with the government of Fidel Castro ... is that he is intransigent on this issue," he said. "He might just use excessive force. I know that I am exposing myself to imprisonment or death."
